extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism and essays; students and critics of poetry, language, and cultural observation
extracted.subtask_short: literary criticism of poets and language
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-essay criteria about what makes poetry and language effective, illustrated by close readings of Burns and Tennyson, an account of slang's role in language evolution, and observational diary/ethnographic notes. Emphasizes authenticity, vernacular, verbal craft, and the social sources of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of native dialect / patois
rubrics_metrics.description: “His brightest hit is his use of the Scotch patois, so full of terms flavor'd like wild fruits or berries.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vernacular gives native spice and an untranslatable twang; examples include Burns' song titles and lines (e.g., 'Wee, sleekit, cowrin, tim'rous beastie:'). The dialect supplies authenticity and vivid local color that other poetic means cannot substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for crudeness and first-draft rawness when authentic
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns' collected works are 'nearly one half first drafts' and 'the frequent crudeness, haste, deficiencies ... prove upon the whole not out of keeping' with his underlying spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-polish material that embodies a direct, farm-field, vernacular veracity; in this poet 'neglect, unfinish, careless nudity, slovenly hiatus' can enhance emotional truth. Anti-pattern: treating such rawness as a mere fault deserving identical correction as with more finished poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match between poet's character/voice and treatment (consonance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crudeness and haste 'are in consonance with the underlying spirit of the pieces' and 'complete the full abandon and veracity' of Burns' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem by how well its form and technical roughness reflect the poet's persona and subject-matter; dissonant polish can damage authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of idiomatic 'snap' and raciness
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly every piece of Burns 'has "snap" and raciness' — idiomatic wit, home-spun sense, 'lance-blade puncturing' satire and lively short addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, idiomatic pieces that deliver instant character, irony, or colloquial wit are a mark of strength. Examples: addresses 'to Mailie and her Lambs', 'to a Mouse', 'to a Haggis'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer, homely poems should please natural taste and be inimitable
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer and more elaborated poems of Burns 'are just such as would please a natural but homely taste, and cute but average intellect, and are inimitable in their way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate extended poems on how well they sustain fresh, racy moral and plot elements accessible to common readers; such works may be spare of profundity yet enduringly admired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of deep, contrasting emotional foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns' basis included 'hypochondria, the blues' and 'the black and desperate background behind those pieces' which gives contrast to riant utterances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and credit an artwork's emotional depth when buoyant surface tones conceal darker underlying feelings; contrast can enrich perceived honesty and complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uninhibited artist-handling and bold freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: In compositions like 'the Jolly Beggars' 'the composer reigns alone, with handling free and broad and true, and is an artist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bold, broad, and free workmanship that risks indelicacy may be an artistic virtue when it serves a commanding individual voice; editions sometimes omit indelicacy, but such omissions can mute the author's power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finest verbalism and the charm of diction (Tennyson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tennyson shows 'how much there is in finest verbalism' — 'latent charm in mere words, cunning collocutions, and in the voice ringing them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciate lyrical poets for verbal mastery and resonant phrasing even when mannerism is pronounced; examples: lines from 'The Passing of Arthur', 'The Lady of Shalott'. Mannerism can be noble and welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of personal moral tone as a poetic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Tennyson 'has been consistent throughout with the native, healthy, patriotic spinal element and promptings of himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poets by the coherence between their moral/psychic stance and their work; a consistent personal line can be a strength even if not radical or democratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of critical, cautionary voices in literature's public function
rubrics_metrics.description: The course of progressive politics is 'so certain and resistless ... that we can well afford the warning calls, threats, checks, neutralizings, in imaginative literature' from voices like Carlyle's and Tennyson's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value literature that functions as a corrective, warning, or counterpoint to prevailing social trends; the social usefulness of such voices is a criterion of worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slang as the germinal, creative element of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang is 'the lawless germinal element, below all words and sentences, and behind all poetry' and is 'the wholesome fermentation' that yields new permanent words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat slang not as merely vulgar but as a productive source for linguistic evolution; many solid words originated in daring slang. Examples: etymologies of 'right', 'wrong', 'integrity', 'spirit'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final authority of language rests with the masses / popular usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Language 'is not an abstract construction of the learn'd, or of dictionary-makers, but ... arising out of the work, needs, ties, joys, affections, tastes, of long generations of humanity' and 'final decisions are made by the masses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate words and forms by actual popular adoption rather than prescriptive norms; nicknames, regional slang, and working-class speech are decisive forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional and frontier speech as especially fecund sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The Western States ... are 'the special areas of slang' with many colorful place-names and coinages (examples: Tumwater, Snohomish, Wahkiakum, Cornucopia, Fairplay, Whiskey Flat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study regional, frontier, and immigrant naming/usage for original, often appropriate coinages; such sources can enrich literary language and cultural study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnographic/portrait recording needs an artist's color and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter argues 'Ten thousand photographs would not have the value of one really finely felt painting. Color is all-important.' An Indian is 'only half an Indian without the blue-black hair and the brilliant eyes shining out of the wonderful dusky ochre and rose complexion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting peoples or cultures, prioritize artistically rendered color, feeling, and selection over mechanical reproduction; one skilled depiction can convey truths photographs may miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and diary writing: vivid sensory detail and exact observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diary passages (comet, moonlit nights, woods, scent of maize-field, katydid song) show the value of precise sensory description: 'The head shows about as big as an ordinary good-sized saucer... the tail some sixty or seventy feet ... so spectral-fierce.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality nature writing relies on exact, sensory-rich observations (sight, smell, sound, timing) and a willingness to linger on the scene; these build immediacy and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological insight from everyday interlocutors' speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversations with a Central Park policeman reveal social judgments: 'the inward caste-spirit of European "aristocracy" pervaded rich America' and that many officials are 'just players in a game.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinary speakers' language and judgments as valid sociological evidence; briefing from non-elites can yield sharp critiques of public life and institutions.
